insights.title: Your kidney filtering has drifted down over two years
insights.found: Your eGFR went from 71 in November 2024 to 64 in 2025 and 58 in November 2026, and your urine albumin rose from 22 to 46 mg/g.
insights.why: An eGFR below 60 with albumin in the urine is chronic kidney disease stage G3a A2. The change in your creatinine between visits is larger than normal day-to-day variation.
insights.means: Your kidneys are working at a little over half of a young adult's level. Your 5-year risk of kidney failure is low (KFRE 0.4%), but the trend is worth slowing.
insights.do: Keep your blood pressure at the target your doctor sets, keep taking losartan, and repeat creatinine, eGFR and urine albumin in 3-6 months at the same lab. Ask your doctor whether a kidney-protecting medicine is right for you.
insights.expected: A steadier eGFR and lower urine albumin at the next tests are the aim.
insights.helps: Slowing the decline protects your kidneys and your heart.

insights.title: Your lipoprotein(a) is above the risk-enhancing level
insights.found: Your Lp(a) is 64 mg/dL. The guideline threshold that counts as a risk-enhancing factor is 50 mg/dL.
insights.why: Lp(a) is mostly inherited and barely changes with diet or exercise. Your father had a heart attack at 58.
insights.means: Lp(a) adds to the risk from your LDL (144 mg/dL) and ApoB (118 mg/dL). It is a reason to treat the other risk factors more firmly, not a diagnosis.
insights.do: Discuss with your doctor how hard to lower LDL and ApoB given your Lp(a), your statin history and your SLCO1B1 result. Close family members may want an Lp(a) test once.
insights.expected: Lp(a) itself is measured once; the plan targets LDL, ApoB and blood pressure.
insights.helps: Knowing this changes how firmly your cholesterol is treated.

insights.title: Your statin muscle aches and your SLCO1B1 result fit together
insights.found: You stopped atorvastatin in July 2023 because of muscle aches. Your genetic test shows SLCO1B1 *1/*5, decreased function.
insights.why: SLCO1B1 carries statins into the liver. Decreased function raises statin levels in the blood, which is linked to muscle symptoms, especially with some statins and higher doses.
insights.means: Statins are not ruled out, but the choice of statin and dose matters for you. Your amlodipine can also raise atorvastatin levels slightly.
insights.do: Before any new cholesterol medicine, show your doctor or pharmacist your SLCO1B1 result. Non-statin options exist too.
insights.expected: A cholesterol plan you can stay on.
insights.helps: Lets your doctor pick a cholesterol treatment that suits your genes.

insights.title: Your blood sugar is in the prediabetes range and rising
insights.found: Fasting glucose 104 mg/dL and HbA1c 5.9%. Two years ago they were 97 mg/dL and 5.6%.
insights.why: Both are in the impaired-fasting-glucose and HbA1c 5.7-6.4% bands. Your mother has type 2 diabetes, and your waist is 89 cm.
insights.means: Your FINDRISC score is 20 of 26 (high) and your Indian Diabetes Risk Score is 70 (high). Prediabetes can often be reversed.
insights.do: Aim for 150 minutes a week of brisk activity (you do about 100), swap some white rice for whole grains or lentils, and recheck HbA1c in 6-12 months.
insights.expected: A lower or steady HbA1c at your next test.
insights.helps: Stopping prediabetes becoming diabetes protects your kidneys too.

insights.title: Your waist size is the most changeable risk you have
insights.found: Waist 89 cm and BMI 27.7. The Asian-Indian cut-points are 80 cm and 23.
insights.why: Fat around the waist drives blood sugar, triglycerides and blood pressure, and it is moving the wrong way (87 cm in 2025).
insights.means: Several of your results (glucose, triglycerides 162, HDL 52, blood pressure) improve together when waist size falls.
insights.do: A modest change, about 3-5 cm off your waist, is a realistic first goal. Your doctor or a dietitian can help plan it.
insights.expected: Better glucose, triglycerides and blood pressure together.
insights.helps: One change that moves many results.

insights.title: Your blood pressure is close to target but not there yet
insights.found: Clinic reading 138/86 in November 2026; home readings average about 136/84. You take amlodipine and losartan.
insights.why: With kidney disease and albumin in the urine, blood pressure targets are usually lower than for other people.
insights.means: Lowering salt is one of the actions the analysis selected for your goal of reducing heart risk. You add salt at the table.
insights.do: Keep a home blood pressure log for a week before your next appointment, cut added salt, and ask your doctor what your target is.
insights.helps: Protects your heart, brain and kidneys at once.

insights.title: Your hs-CRP suggests low-grade inflammation
insights.found: hs-CRP 2.4 mg/L, up from 1.6 in 2024. The heart-risk threshold is 2.0 mg/L.
insights.why: Low-grade inflammation adds to heart risk. Waist size, poor sleep and inactivity all raise it.
insights.means: It is a risk marker, not an infection. A single value can be raised by a cold, so it is best repeated.
insights.do: Repeat hs-CRP when you are well, together with your next lipid test.
insights.expected: A lower value as waist and activity improve.

insights.title: Low vitamin D and thinner bones
insights.found: Vitamin D 18 ng/mL (down from 24 in 2024) although you take 2000 IU a day. Your DXA scan in September 2026 showed osteopenia (spine T-score -1.6).
insights.why: After menopause bone loss speeds up. Your grandmother had a hip fracture.
insights.means: Osteopenia is not osteoporosis, but it is the time to protect your bones.
insights.do: Ask your doctor whether your vitamin D dose should change, keep calcium-rich foods in your diet, and add strength or weight-bearing exercise twice a week.
insights.expected: A higher vitamin D level and steady bone density on the next scan.

insights.title: Your uric acid is slightly high
insights.found: Uric acid 6.4 mg/dL; the female threshold for raised urate is 6.2 mg/dL.
insights.why: Uric acid rises as kidney filtering falls and with insulin resistance.
insights.means: You have no gout. This is information to watch, not a reason for treatment on its own.
insights.do: Recheck with your next kidney tests.
insights.expected: Stable or lower with weight and glucose changes.

insights.title: Your liver scarring score is reassuring
insights.found: Your FIB-4 score is 1.10, below 1.3, so advanced liver scarring is unlikely. ALT is 31 U/L, slightly above a South Indian healthy range for women.
insights.why: A mildly raised ALT with a larger waist can mean some fat in the liver.
insights.means: The scarring score is good news. The ALT is worth watching as you work on waist size.
insights.do: Recheck ALT with your next blood tests.
insights.expected: ALT falls as waist size falls.

insights.title: Mild low mood, mild worry and short sleep
insights.found: PHQ-9 score 6 (mild), GAD-7 score 5 (mild). You sleep about 6.3 hours a night and wake once or twice.
insights.why: You are caring for an elderly relative and rate your stress 6 out of 10.
insights.means: These are screening scores, not a diagnosis. Sleep is one of your lower Life's Essential 8 scores (70).
insights.do: Tell your doctor how you are feeling. A regular wind-down and 7 hours in bed are a good start.
insights.expected: Better sleep and energy over a few weeks.

ask.a: Your PhenoAge, a research-only estimate built from 9 routine blood results, is 55.8 years; your calendar age is 56. It is not a clinical measure and was computed with all 9 inputs present.

ask.q: What is my heart attack and stroke risk?
ask.a: Your 10-year risk is about 3% by SCORE2 and the Pooled Cohort Equations, 5.1% by PREVENT (total cardiovascular disease) and 6.0% by QRISK3. These are different models fitted to different populations, so they are shown side by side, not averaged. The WHO 2019 model could not be calibrated for your region.

ask.q: What is my lifetime heart risk?
ask.a: LIFE-CVD2 estimates an 11% risk of a heart attack or stroke before age 80, and about 32 more years free of heart disease, recalibrated to the low-risk European region where you live.

Your eGFR is 58 (stage G3a) and urine albumin 46 mg/g (A2). eGFR was 71 in 2024 and 64 in 2025. The kidney failure risk equation gives 0.1% over 2 years and 0.4% over 5 years, which is low, but the trend is worth slowing.

No. Your HbA1c is 5.9% and fasting glucose 104 mg/dL, which is the prediabetes range. FINDRISC scores you 20 of 26 (high) and the Indian Diabetes Risk Score 70 (high), largely because of your waist size and your mother's diabetes.
Your Lp(a) is 64 mg/dL, above the 50 mg/dL level that guidelines treat as a risk-enhancing factor. It is mostly inherited, so the plan focuses on lowering LDL, ApoB and blood pressure more firmly.

ask.q: Can I take a statin again?
ask.a: Possibly. Your muscle aches on atorvastatin fit your SLCO1B1 decreased-function result. Your doctor can choose a statin and dose with that in mind, or a non-statin option. This is a decision for your doctor, not something to change on your own.

You have tested results for SLCO1B1 (*1/*5, decreased function), CYP2C19 (*1/*2, intermediate metaboliser), CYP2D6 and CYP2C9 (normal). You also carry one HFE H63D variant, classed as benign, and APOE e3/e4. Genes we have not tested are reported as untested, never as normal.
It is close but not at target: 138/86 in clinic and about 136/84 at home. With kidney disease, targets are usually lower. Cutting added salt was one of the actions selected for you.

ask.q: Why is my vitamin D low when I take a supplement?
ask.a: Your level is 18 ng/mL on 2000 IU a day, down from 24 in 2024. Your DXA scan shows osteopenia. Ask your doctor whether the dose should change.
Your FIB-4 score is 1.10, which makes advanced liver scarring unlikely. ALT is 31 U/L, slightly above a South Indian healthy range for women, which is worth rechecking.

ask.q: How are my mood and sleep?
ask.a: PHQ-9 is 6 and GAD-7 is 5, both mild. You sleep about 6.3 hours on your tracker. These are screening scores, not a diagnosis.

ask.q: What is my Life's Essential 8 score?
ask.a: 65 out of 100. Not smoking scored 100; activity 80; sleep and BMI 70; glucose 60; diet and blood pressure 50; blood lipids 40.
Over 28 days: a median of 6,400 steps a day, resting heart rate 68, sleep 6.3 hours, HRV 29 ms and SpO2 96.5%. Wearable data is shown separately and never enters a risk equation.

The medicine screen found no interaction rated major between your current medicines (amlodipine and losartan are listed together in the medical medical references without a severity). It notes that amlodipine can slightly raise atorvastatin levels if a statin is restarted, and that losartan with a potassium-sparing medicine such as finerenone would need potassium monitoring.

ask.q: What did the drug-discovery analysis find?
ask.a: It listed 17 research targets linked to your conditions (for example AGTR1, HMGCR, PCSK9, SLC5A2 and APOE). It profiled no compounds and ran no docking, because those steps need online databases that were switched off for this run. This is research only, not treatment.

genes.function: Binds to transferrin receptor (TFR) and reduces its affinity for iron-loaded transferrin.
APOE is an apolipoprotein, a protein associating with lipid particles, that mainly functions in lipoprotein-mediated lipid transport between organs via the plasma and interstitial fluids.
Electrogenic Na(+)-coupled sugar symporter that actively transports D-glucose at the plasma membrane, with a Na(+) to sugar coupling ratio of 1:1.
Receptor for both mineralocorticoids (MC) such as aldosterone and glucocorticoids (GC) such as corticosterone or cortisol.
Receptor for angiotensin II, a vasoconstricting peptide, which acts as a key regulator of blood pressure and sodium retention by the kidney.

Catalyzes the conversion of (3S)-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) to mevalonic acid, the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of cholesterol and other isoprenoids, thus plays a critical role in cellular cholesterol homeostasis.
Mediates the Na(+)-independent uptake of organic anions.
Type IV collagen is the major structural component of glomerular basement membranes (GBM), forming a 'chicken-wire' meshwork together with laminins, proteoglycans and entactin/nidogen.
PPIase that catalyzes the cis-trans isomerization of proline imidic peptide bonds in oligopeptides and may therefore assist protein folding.

Metabolic-stress sensing protein kinase that phosphorylates the alpha subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (EIF2S1/eIF-2-alpha) in response to various stress, such as unfolded protein response (UPR).
Deacetylates a wide range of non-histone substrates.
Catalyzes the hydrolysis of glycosphingolipids and participates in their degradation in the lysosome.

Dipeptidyl carboxypeptidase that removes dipeptides from the C-terminus of a variety of circulating hormones, such as angiotensin I, bradykinin or enkephalins, thereby playing a key role in the regulation of blood pressure, electrolyte homeostasis or synaptic plasticity.
